resources.string: Enter your maximum heart rate to see training load, form and zones. Resting heart rate is measured while you sleep.
Breathing rate during sleep is clearly above usual, a common early sign of illness.

Readiness combines last night's measurements with your recent training, each compared with your own normal rather than with population averages.

# What goes in
- HRV, 35 %: the 7-day average of nightly HRV against your normal range from the last 60 days.
- Sleep, 25 %: last night's sleep score and the average of the last three nights.
- Resting heart rate, 20 %: last night against your usual.
- Training, 20 %: form against a band that grows with your fitness.

# Safeguards
- While your HRV is below its normal range, readiness stays below "Ready to train", as HRV-guided training studies recommend.
- A breathing rate clearly above usual, together with low HRV or a raised resting heart rate, holds readiness at 40 or below: a common early sign of illness.

# How much to trust it
The HRV comparison has the strongest research behind it. The weights are PacingLab's own choice, not a validated score. A first score appears after 7 nights of HRV and is marked provisional: with only a week, last night can be compared with the range seen so far, but the week's trend cannot yet be told apart from it. From 14 nights the score is settled; it keeps improving over four to eight weeks.

# The week
The small chart shows the score of each of the last seven days, computed from the data up to that day, on the bands of the three levels: take it easy below 50, train with care from 50, ready to train from 70.

resources.string: Heart rate over the workout, coloured by zone

Your own answer, once in the morning, from 1 (exhausted) to 5 (fully rested).

How rested you feel is the one part of sleep health a watch cannot measure. In training research, simple daily ratings like this one follow training load at least as well as most measurements (Saw 2016).

PacingLab keeps your answers with the night they follow. Once you answer, the card leaves Today; the sleep screen shows the answer and lets you change it, for any morning, at the bottom under How you felt and the score. Once a few weeks have collected, that card shows how well the sleep score matches how you feel.
How hard was the gym session?

One tap for how hard the whole session felt, from 1 (very, very easy) to 10 (maximal).\n\nHeart rate reacts little to lifting, so the rating is what gives a gym session its training load: the rating times the minutes, known as session RPE (Foster 2001). Only gym sessions ask, and only until the day after. The rating can be changed on the session\'s page.

Last night's overnight measures, each against your own usual range (where 80 % of your nights fell), as on the Sleep screen.

Any measure leaves its range now and then. When two or more do on the same night, the card warns, as Apple's Vitals app does: an illness starting, alcohol, travel or a hard block of training are the usual reasons. It is a prompt to take it easy, not a diagnosis.

SpO2 and skin temperature come only from the Google Health API. Tap for the Sleep screen.
%1$s is outside your usual range. One measure on its own often is.

Forecast by Open-Meteo (open-meteo.com, CC BY 4.0), which blends the national weather services' models; in Denmark that includes DMI's.

Only your approximate position, rounded to about 1 km, is sent, with no other data. A forecast is reused for 20 minutes while you stay nearby.

Feels like combines temperature, wind and humidity. Dew point is the measure of humidity that matters when running in heat: the higher it is, the less your sweat evaporates and cools you. Wind is in metres per second. Each hour shows its chance of rain from 20 %% up.
The forecast needs your approximate location. Only a position rounded to about 1 km is sent to Open-Meteo.
